## The sharp that nobody printed

In D major, a written F sounds as F-sharp even when there's no sharp anywhere
near that note head. Two marks at the head of the system said so, once, and
they keep saying it for the rest of the piece. A natural sign can shout them
down for a bar. Later Fs in that same bar inherit the shouting. Then the barline
arrives and the signature quietly takes over again.

So what a printed page leaves out matters as much as what it prints. A *key
signature* maps letter names onto default sharp or flat alterations. An
*accidental* is a local override, scoped to one bar and, in this decoder, to one
letter at one octave. If you've ever debugged a config file that inherits from a
global default, gets patched per environment, and then gets overridden by a
command-line flag, you already know the shape of this problem. Resolve the
layers in the wrong order and an unmarked note comes out natural when the page
meant it sharp.

## Two bars under one standing rule

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 88
use_synth :piano

semitones = {c: 0, d: 2, e: 4, f: 5, g: 7, a: 9, b: 11}
key_signature = {f: 1, c: 1}  # D major

define :resolve_note do |event, key_signature, local, semitones|
  scope_key = [event[:letter], event[:octave]]
  local[scope_key] = event[:accidental] if event.key?(:accidental)
  alteration = local.fetch(scope_key, key_signature.fetch(event[:letter], 0))
  12 * (event[:octave] + 1) + semitones[event[:letter]] + alteration
end

bars = [
  [
    {letter: :f, octave: 4, duration: 1},
    {letter: :g, octave: 4, duration: 1},
    {letter: :f, octave: 4, duration: 1, accidental: 0},
    {letter: :f, octave: 4, duration: 1}
  ],
  [
    {letter: :f, octave: 4, duration: 1},
    {letter: :c, octave: 5, duration: 1},
    {letter: :c, octave: 5, duration: 1, accidental: -1},
    {letter: :d, octave: 5, duration: 1}
  ]
]

bars.each do |bar|
  local = {}
  bar.each do |event|
    pitch = resolve_note(event, key_signature, local, semitones)
    puts "#{event} -> #{pitch}"
    play pitch, release: 0.7
    sleep event[:duration]
  end
end
```

Bar one holds three Fs. The first carries no sign, the second carries a natural,
and the third carries nothing at all. Sharp or natural on that third one? Decide
before you read the log.

Here's what the resolver does. The first F takes its sharp from the signature.
The explicit natural writes zero into the local slot for F4, so the third F stays
natural without a second sign on the page. Bar two builds a fresh `local` hash
and F-sharp is back. The C-flat later in that bar runs the same precedence the
other way: a local value replacing a sharp default with a flat.

## Break the scope on purpose

1. Change the signature to `{b: -1, e: -1}` for B-flat major. Flats are negative
   and sharps positive in one alteration field, so the resolver needs no new
   branch to handle them.
2. Add F5 straight after the F4 natural. Because the local key carries the
   octave, F5 still inherits F-sharp from the signature. Now delete `octave`
   from `scope_key` and run it again. You'll hear the F4 natural bleed into a
   register the page never touched.
3. Add an explicit sharp after the natural in the same bar. The later sign
   overwrites the earlier F4 assignment, which is how bar-local state is
   supposed to behave until the barline clears it.

## Innermost scope wins

`resolve_note` searches from the most local information outward. An accidental
on the current event updates bar state first. Bar state beats the key signature,
and the signature beats the table of natural pitch classes. Two nested `fetch`
calls put that fallback order on one line, where you can read it, instead of
scattering it through special cases.

Letter and alteration stay separate all the way through. F-sharp and G-flat
resolve to the same MIDI number while keeping different letters and different
signs, and you need that difference for correct interval names, key-aware
analysis, and honest comparison with a printed edition. Collapse both to pitch
class 6 early and you can never reconstruct which one the page showed you.

Published notation has rules this example doesn't reach: conventions for
cancelling accidentals, and the treatment of notes tied across a barline. The
resolver states a smaller model and shows you its edge. Extend it when a real
source hands you a case it can't express, so every new branch answers an
observed problem.

Key signatures store defaults by letter, which brings the circle of fifths
straight back into the data model. D major sharpens F and C. It doesn't announce
anonymous pitch classes 6 and 1. Keep the written letter after resolution and a
diagnostic can still tell a deliberate enharmonic spelling from a typo.

## Write the resolver yourself

Write `resolve_bar(events, key_signature)` so it returns new hashes carrying a
MIDI `:note` while preserving letter, octave, start, duration, and any
accidental. Scope the bar-local overrides with `key = [event[:letter],
event[:octave]]`, the way the code above does.

Feed it a four-bar phrase containing a sharp signature, a natural override, a
repeated affected note, the same letter in another octave, and a barline reset.
Print each source event beside its resolved form. Read the two columns together:
one tells you what the notation said, the other tells you which layer supplied
the final alteration.
